nodes.label: Rogers Brubaker
nodes.date_label: Citizenship and Nationhood in France and Germany (1992) · Nationalism Reframed (1996) · “Beyond ‘Identity’,” with Frederick Cooper (2000)
nodes.description: Investigates citizenship, nationhood and the analytical work performed by identity categories. With Frederick Cooper, he distinguishes people’s use of identity in political life from an analyst’s assumption that everyone possesses an identity or belongs to an already coherent group. Their alternative vocabulary separates identification, categorization, self-understanding and variable groupness. Their account of states emphasizes the power to impose administrative categories while refusing to equate that power with complete control of self-identification. Historical comparisons of France/Germany and postimperial Europe form part of this cross-disciplinary research.

nodes.label: Ernest Gellner
nodes.date_label: Thought and Change (1964) · Nations and Nationalism (1983) · Encounters with Nationalism (1994) · Warwick reply, “Do nations have navels?” (1995)
nodes.description: Relates nationalism to the mobility, specialized work and expensive shared literate culture of modern societies. In his Warwick reply, cultural continuity is possible but contingent rather than necessary to national formation. He accepts that preindustrial cultures could be consciously valued and sometimes politically expressed; this qualification complicates a simple claim that the past never matters. Anthony D. Smith’s opening challenges the sufficiency of a general modernist account for particular nationalisms. Their disagreement concerns explanatory weight and historical specificity, not a settled opposition between an ahistorical modernism and an unchanging ethnic essence.

nodes.label: Anne McClintock
nodes.date_label: “Family Feuds: Gender, Nationalism and the Family” (1993) · Imperial Leather (1995) · Dangerous Liaisons: coedited collection (1997)
nodes.description: Analyzes nationalism through gendered access to political agency and the family images that make hierarchy appear natural. The selected opening of “Family Feuds” asks how women become symbolic bearers of national belonging while access to rights and resources remains uneven. Its family-trope discussion examines how national and imperial narratives turn social hierarchy and violent historical change into seemingly organic development. In a specifically named response to Edward Said, she retains his distinction between filiation and affiliation but argues that familial images persist inside new national, bureaucratic and imperial institutions. These are her situated historical interpretations, not universal facts established merely by the force of a theoretical formulation.

nodes.label: Marcel Mauss
nodes.date_label: “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice,” with Henri Hubert (1899) · Sacrifice essay reprinted in Mélanges d’histoire des religions (1909) · “Essai sur le don” (1925) · The Gift: Jane I. Guyer’s expanded English edition (2016)
nodes.description: Examines obligations and ritual relations across law, religion and economy. The selected Gift introduction asks why apparently voluntary gifts entail giving back and treats exchange as embedded in several institutions rather than as isolated transactions between self-contained individuals. His comparative programme identifies selected areas and documentary limits; its historical vocabulary and sweeping formulations remain attributable to its period. With Henri Hubert, the earlier sacrifice essay offers a provisional account of ritual mediation between sacred and profane. The two projects have different questions and credits, and later translations or collections do not make them interchangeable.

nodes.label: Mary Douglas
nodes.date_label: Purity and Danger (1966) · The World of Goods, with Baron Isherwood (1979) · How Institutions Think (1986) · Lancaster interview on classification and the body (1987)
nodes.description: Studies classification, bodily symbolism and the social work of goods. In the selected 1987 interview, she places her account of the body within a Durkheimian classificatory conversation while resisting the interviewer’s imposed theoretical alternatives. The interviewer’s summaries and her responses remain distinct. Featherstone and Turner’s later introduction reads her collaboration with Baron Isherwood as locating consumption within systems of meaning rather than merely a division between necessities and luxuries. That particular named reading supplies the consumption claim; it does not become a new claim to have read the whole World of Goods.

nodes.label: Anthony Giddens
nodes.date_label: The Constitution of Society (1984) · The Consequences of Modernity (1990) · Modernity and Self-Identity (1991)
nodes.description: Develops structuration as an account of how social practices reproduce and transform the rules and resources on which they depend. Structure is both enabling and constraining, not merely an outside force confronting a free individual. The selected chapter also makes time and space constitutive of social practice: purposeful conduct unfolds through embodied, situated activity, and its consequences exceed what actors intend. This avoids treating either an individual subject or a social whole as a self-sufficient starting point. The earlier Sewell abstract identifies a later reformulation, while its limited reading does not establish every detail of that criticism.

nodes.label: Gilles Deleuze
nodes.date_label: Mille plateaux, with Félix Guattari (1980) · Foucault (1986) · A Thousand Plateaus: translation and foreword Brian Massumi (1987) · “Post-scriptum sur les sociétés de contrôle” (1990) · “Postscript on the Societies of Control”: English translation (1992)
nodes.description: Uses the postscript on control to propose a historical distinction between bounded disciplinary institutions and continuously modulating controls. His account explicitly works through Foucault’s analysis of enclosure while arguing that newer forms of control alter its organization. Codes, access permissions, computers and changing corporate forms become analytical examples, but the essay rejects a simple claim that machines determine society. This is an attributed and contestable periodization, not a statement that every prison, factory or disciplinary practice has vanished. Joint books with Félix Guattari retain their coauthorship and their translation credits rather than being absorbed into a solo Deleuze bibliography.

nodes.label: Anthony D. Smith
nodes.date_label: The Ethnic Origins of Nations (1986) · National Identity (1991) · Warwick opening, “Nations and their pasts” (1995) · Nationalism and Modernism (1998)
nodes.description: Explains particular nationalisms through ethnic ties, inherited memories, myths and symbols while acknowledging the modernity of most nations and nationalist movements. His Warwick opening praises Gellner’s contribution but argues that a general account of modernization leaves the content and intensity of particular cases unexplained. Smith explicitly declines to require one definite antecedent ethnic community for every nation. His ethno-symbolic approach therefore differs from a claim that all modern nations are unchanged survivals of antiquity. The debate with Gellner is presented through the participants’ own formulations, including their concessions and disagreements.

edges.relationship: With Frederick Cooper, distinguishes identity as a political/practical category from the analytical processes of identification, categorization and variable groupness.
edges.evidence_note: Primary article opening pp. 1–2 and selected “In other words” / “Identification and categorization” section pp. 14–17 read in an explicitly identified OCR mirror. This is conceptual differentiation, not a dismissal of identity politics or all historical experience.

edges.relationship: With Cooper, analyzes the state’s power to impose classifications while distinguishing external categorization from people’s self-identifications.
edges.evidence_note: Joint primary pp. 15–17: state resources support official categories, but states do not monopolize identification and categories do not automatically produce homogeneous groups. Historical examples/referenced authors were not independently audited.

edges.relationship: Links nationalism to modern mobility and mastery of a shared literate culture maintained through political and educational institutions.
edges.evidence_note: Retained primary Gellner reply, with newly inspected central paragraphs on mobility/high culture and contingent continuities. These are his explanatory claims, not a universal outcome or an assertion that cultures lacked any earlier political expression.

edges.relationship: Contests the explanatory necessity of premodern cultural continuity while acknowledging that such continuity sometimes exists.
edges.evidence_note: Direct named Warwick reply to Smith’s opening; both are primary debate statements. Gellner’s provocative primordialist label is not adopted as Smith’s self-definition; Gellner explicitly concedes contingent continuities. No collective nationalism-field arrow is changed.

edges.relationship: Examines unequal national agency and the use of women as symbolic bearers of national belonging.
edges.evidence_note: Primary pp. 61–63, with pp. 64–65 family/hierarchy context read in Wisconsin author-hosted scan text. General “all nations” formulations remain McClintock’s claims; no universal empirical certification or denial of women’s political action.

edges.relationship: Retains Said’s filiation/affiliation distinction while disputing a linear replacement of family relations by nonfamilial institutional orders.
edges.evidence_note: Specifically named primary response, printed p. 64 with pp. 63–65 context. She argues that familial images were reinvented within national and imperial institutions. Said’s underlying passage is not newly collated and the critique is not generalized to all his work.

edges.relationship: Studies obligations to give back and the intersection of legal, religious and economic relations in apparently voluntary exchanges.
edges.evidence_note: New primary digital pp. 7–9 read: Programme, Méthode suivie and opening Prestation/Don/Potlatch. Selected-area comparison and local documentary specificity retained; ethnographic cases and universal market/reciprocity claims not independently established.

edges.relationship: Examines the body as a resource for social classification, while distinguishing that project from the interviewer’s phenomenological framing.
